title: Aad sach: the meaning
hook: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true hereafter, says Nanak

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, Naanak hosee bhee sach. Your line was aad sach. Did you say it as you woke? Day one hundred sixty-two.

We use the word true in two different ways. A true statement: it happens to be so. It's raining. It's Tuesday. That kind of true can change by tomorrow. And a true friend: the one who stays. That kind of true is about lasting. It's the friend who still shows up after the move, the divorce, the bad year. Guru Nanak's salok uses the second kind. Yesterday you said it four times. Today, what it's saying.
screen: `TRUE: IT HAPPENS TO BE SO.` → `TRUE: IT STAYS.` → `TODAY, THE MEANING.`

segments.voice: Sach is truth, the true. In Gurbani it's more than a correct fact. It's a name for the One: the reality that doesn't wear out. The Mool Mantar said it first: sat naam, truth is the name. Now the salok spells out what that means, in four steps. Macauliffe's translation keeps close to the Gurmukhi, and in plain words it says: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true even now, and, says Nanak, true it shall be hereafter. Aad: the beginning, before anything was. Jugaad: through the ages, the long cycles of time that Indian thought counts in. Hai bhee: is, even now, at this moment. Hosee bhee: will be, also, ever after. That small word bhee, also, even, is the quiet hero. True then, and also now. True now, and also later. Nothing about the passing of time takes anything away. Notice what isn't there. No argument. No proof. Guru Nanak doesn't reason his way to it; he states it, the way you'd name a mountain you can see. Japji will spend thirty-eight pauris on how a person comes to live inside that truth. And notice the name in the middle: Nanak. The Guru signs his hymns with his name, and the later Gurus in the Granth sign theirs as Nanak too. It's a signature, and a witness: this is what Nanak saw. Why begin here? Because everything that follows, a restless mind, a changing world, fame and loss, stands in front of something that doesn't change. That's the ground Japji is built on.
screen: `SACH — THE TRUE THAT LASTS.` · `BEGINNING, AGES, NOW, HEREAFTER.` · `BHEE — ALSO, EVEN NOW.` · `NANAK SIGNS AS WITNESS.` · then, large: `SACH.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly. Picture yourself at seven years old. Then at fifteen. Then a year ago. Then now. So much has changed: your face, your work, your opinions, your address. Look for one thing that hasn't. Maybe a way you love people. A stubborn honesty. A sense of wonder. A fear you've always faced anyway. Find it, and name it quietly to yourself. Something true then, and true now. If you pray, you can hold it up to the One the salok calls true. The bell holds the time.
Sach. Truth, the true that lasts: true in the beginning, through the ages, now, and hereafter.
Your line: true then, true now. Tell one person today something true you've always meant but rarely said. Day one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the salok on the eternal truth every morning after the Mool Mantar, and sach, the True, is one of the most common names for God in the Guru Granth Sahib.

match.prompt: match the words to their meaning.

myth: in Gurbani, sach only means a correct fact
it's a name for the One, the reality that doesn't wear out.
the salok argues its way to its claim
there's no argument; Guru Nanak states it, like naming a mountain.
later Gurus also sign their hymns as Nanak
the name is a signature and a witness.

fork.setup: the salok names four times. which one is missing?
fork.reveal: beginning, ages, now, hereafter: the verse doesn't need a personal date; it covers all time.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sach, truth, the True. the small mark under the last letter is mostly silent.

trapdoor: what you thought: true, as in not false.
what it means: the true that lasts: the One, true in the beginning, through the ages, now and hereafter.
what a scholar hears: sach is kin to Sanskrit satya and to sat in sat naam; bhee, also, carries the claim across time.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (salok after the Mool Mantar)
